---
title: "How to design an RCT"
---

::: {.team-note}
#### Summary
This page explains the basics of how to design randomised controlled trials.
:::

A well-designed randomised controlled trial does not begin with randomisation — it begins with a clear understanding of what the programme is trying to achieve and why. The seven steps below set out the preparatory work that makes randomisation meaningful and the results credible. Managing Authorities are encouraged to work through them in sequence, ideally before the first call for applications is launched.

::: {.cards}
::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 1: Develop a preliminary Theory of Change](02.01-toc.qmd)

Map the causal logic of your intervention — from inputs to long-term goals — and make the assumptions explicit.
:::
::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 2: Define learning questions](02.02-eval_questions.qmd)

Formulate the specific questions the evaluation is designed to answer, grounded in the Theory of Change.
:::

::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 3: Determine relevant indicators](02.04-indicators.qmd)

Select the outcome indicators that will be used to measure change across each level of the Theory of Change.
:::

::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 4: Assess feasibility of conducting an RCT](02.03-assess.qmd)

Check whether the conditions for a valid RCT are in place — oversubscription, timing, legal basis, and political buy-in.
:::

::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 5: Identify available data sources](02.05-data_sources.qmd)

Decide whether to rely on primary data, administrative data, or a combination — and map what is already available.
:::

::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 6: Collect data](02.06-data_collect.qmd)

Design and implement the data collection — surveys, administrative data access, and quality controls.
:::

::: {.card-e}

#### [Step 7: Ensure high-quality data](02.07-data_quality.qmd)

Put in place the checks needed to detect and address data quality problems before analysis begins.
:::

:::
